source.title: From Assumptions to Actions: Turning LLM Reasoning into Uncertainty-Aware Planning for Embodied Agents
source.authors: Seung-hun Seo; Soobin Lim; SeongRae Noh; Haneul Kim; HyeongYeop Kang

record.file_problem: None; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper varies model capacity and reasoning depth and reports effects on embodied-task performance, a different measure from pretraining loss. This bears on downstream performance versus scale (V6), but it does not measure the original loss-scaling laws.
record.gate_note: The paper cites Kaplan et al. and discusses model scaling, but does not measure held-out cross-entropy, training tokens or compute, fit power laws, or test compute-optimal allocation. Its own relevant result is an ablation varying Gemma3 capacity and GPT-OSS:20B reasoning depth for C-WAH task performance. Exact points in Figure 3 are not stated in the text.
record.test_reason: This is an embodied multi-agent planning paper. Its only scale-related result is an ablation in Section 5.2 and Figure 3. That ablation compares a Planner-only variant against PCE across Gemma3 4B, 12B and 27B, and across GPT-OSS:20B reasoning levels. Its purpose is to show that PCE's gains add to scaling. It has three model sizes, gives values only in a figure, and offers only the qualitative statement that improvements are 'only modest'. It fits no trend and makes no test of predictability. It measures no pretraining loss, tokens or compute. It therefore does not bear on whether downstream performance improves predictably with scale (V6), or on any other version. The capacity trend is recorded under fits_no_version.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors say that scaling capacity or reasoning depth alone gives only modest Planner-only gains. They also say those scaling gains persist when PCE is applied, and that PCE raises performance at every scale, so the two are complementary. The record omits the claim that scaling gains persist under PCE.
record.recipe_differences: The paper evaluates embodied-agent task performance using prompted LLM planners, rather than measuring held-out pretraining loss or fitting scaling laws. It varies model capacity and inference reasoning depth, not training parameters, tokens or compute.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported scaling result is for the Planner-only variant on C-WAH; PCE is described as faster across the tested scales. Reasoning depth is varied separately for GPT-OSS:20B.

fits_no_version.finding: In C-WAH, Planner-only Total Steps improve only modestly as Gemma3 grows from 4B to 12B to 27B. PCE is faster at every size (figure only).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Scaling the LLM backbone of an embodied planner yields only modest gains in task efficiency, and these gains are additive with structured uncertainty handling.

fits_no_version.finding: In C-WAH, Planner-only performance improves modestly as GPT-OSS:20B reasoning depth rises from Low to Medium to High.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Increasing inference-time reasoning depth yields modest gains in embodied planning efficiency in the tested setting.

record.code_released: not stated; the authors say code and reproduction instructions are included in anonymized supplementary materials.
record.problems: The scaling ablation's exact results are presented only in Figure 3 and are not given numerically in the text. The scaling evidence is limited to embodied task performance on C-WAH and does not measure pretraining loss or establish predictability.
record.rows_left_out: No separate rows for PCE capacity-scale points: the relevant text reports the comparative conclusion that PCE remains faster, while the claim-specific scaling result is the Planner-only trend. Other benchmark comparisons and user-study results do not test the claim versions.

untested.parts: All parts: no pretraining loss and no parameter, token or compute sweeps.
All parts: no fits and no extrapolation.
All parts: no power-law fits in other regimes.
Whether downstream performance follows a predictable function of scale or loss. There is only a three-point capacity sweep described qualitatively, with no fit.
All parts: no fitting choices examined.

record.verdict_notes: The paper cites Kaplan et al. only to say 'scaling model capacity improves performance'. Appendix A.10 asserts that stronger backbones such as GPT-4o mini outperform Gemma. That comparison confounds model family with size, and it is not a scaling test.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out pretraining loss versus parameters, tokens or compute; bottleneck conditions; power-law form across several orders of magnitude.
Whether fits from small pretraining runs predict much larger runs.
Compute-optimal parameter/token allocations and their growth with training compute.
Effects of depth, width and other architecture details at fixed parameter count.
Power-law behavior in other modalities or training regimes.

The paper measures embodied-task performance in a limited setting, not performance across a broad set of downstream tasks or its relation to pretraining loss. It does not fit or test a quantitative predictive relationship.
Dependence of loss-law exponents or compute-optimal splits on fitting choices and setup.

tranche.reason: The capacity and reasoning sweeps establish that PCE's performance advantage complements scaling. They do not fit or validate a scaling law or establish predictable downstream performance.
